title: Facilitating Client Self-Challenge: From New Perspectives to New Behavior
overview: Chapter 6 explains how helpers invite clients to challenge themselves so that they move from self-limiting blind spots to new perspectives and new behaviour. Egan first sets out self-challenge as a stronger 'nudge' within choice architecture, insists that all effective helping mixes support and challenge, and states the goals of challenging. He lists the targets of self-challenge: self-defeating mind-sets (including Ellis's irrational beliefs and Sternberg's fallacies), internal behaviour, emotional expression, external behaviour, distorted views of the world, discrepancies, unused strengths and the predictable dishonesties of everyday life, closing with Hayes's ACT. He then examines blind spots: lack of awareness, failure to think things through, self-deception, choosing to stay in the dark, and knowing but not caring. Finally he presents the skills for helping clients challenge blind spots: indirect ones (advanced empathy in four forms, information sharing, helper self-disclosure with guidelines) and more direct ones (suggestions and recommendations, confrontation), ending with encouragement and motivational interviewing.
objectives: Explain self-challenge, its link to choice architecture, and why helping must mix support and challenge.
State the two goals of challenging and list every target area of self-challenge with examples.
Describe Ellis's irrational beliefs, Sternberg's fallacies and schemas as self-defeating mind-sets.
Explain the predictable dishonesties of everyday life (distortions, games, excuses) and Hayes's ACT caution.
Define blind spots and distinguish their five kinds, using Van Hecke, Goleman, Giannetti and Heffernan.
Explain advanced empathy and its four forms, including the six uses of educated hunches.
Describe information sharing and helper self-disclosure with their guidelines and cautions.
Evaluate suggestions/recommendations, confrontation and encouragement (including motivational interviewing) as direct approaches.

sections.heading: Self-Challenge: The Basic Concept
sections.detailed:
Egan opens Part II's treatment of challenge by linking it to change: helping is about change, and change means making choices. Chapters 6 and 7 are about helping clients make life-enhancing choices. They are a form of the "choice architecture" introduced in Chapter 5, and inviting clients to challenge themselves is described as a stronger version of the "nudging" discussed there. The key framing question is how therapy can be set up so that clients discover and use the resources inside and around them. Helping clients place demands on themselves may be one of the most valuable things a helper does.

Egan admits that little current therapy research looks directly at choice and self-challenge. But humanity has built up a huge literature on bringing out the best in ourselves, from the Bible to modern writing on healthy physical, psychological, social and moral lifestyles. He argues it would be hubris to insist that this accumulated wisdom must pass randomized clinical trials before it can be used. This is not a rejection of evidence-based practice; it is a call to balance it with the practice-based evidence that has grown up over centuries. Self-challenge helps clients bring the good, the better and the best in themselves to bear on problems and unused opportunities, and it promotes self-responsibility and self-determination.

Life is full of conflict and conflict involves challenging; failing to challenge can be devastating. Egan's example is the operating room: when nurses and technicians do not challenge surgeons' mistakes, patients, hospitals and surgeons all suffer. Hospitals have therefore tried to change OR culture (Carter; Landro). In one survey, 60% of respondents agreed that it was hard to speak up about a patient-care problem in their ORs. Too much is at stake not to challenge.

The communication skills already covered (empathy, probing, summarizing) can help clients engage in reality testing. Clients who cannot or do not challenge themselves do themselves no favour; reasonable self-challenge is part of maturity, and the Chapter 2 values of self-responsibility and a bias for action demand it. The case of Belinda, an overloaded mother of three, illustrates self-initiated self-challenge: after reading an article about middle-class parents who want independent children yet do everything for them and overprotect them, she recognises herself and her husband Gene in it, and both join counselling.

Such self-initiated challenge is ideal but uncommon. Because helping at its best is a constructive social-influence process, some form of challenge is central to it. This is not a retreat from the book's pro-client stance; it underlines collaboration in making self-challenge part of helping. All effective helping mixes support and challenge: challenge without support is harsh and unjustified, while support without challenge can be empty and counterproductive.

Martin (1994) suggested that the helping dialogue adds most value when clients find it relevant, helpful, interested and supportive, yet somehow discordant with their current theories of themselves. Trevino (1996) made the same point in cross-cultural counselling: congruence between counsellor and client strengthens the relationship, while discrepancy facilitates change, and Claiborn's (1982) review concluded that presenting discrepant views helps outcomes by changing how clients construe problems and consider solutions. Challenge supplies that discordant note.

Egan deliberately uses "challenge" rather than the harder-edged "confrontation", because people find confronting and being confronted unpleasant but will accept the softer yet still edgy idea of challenge; "self-challenge" sounds constructive. Finn (2005) stresses compassion and firmness: helpers sometimes have to say hard things in plain, non-judgemental language, which demands courage and wisdom; or, better, help clients say hard things to themselves. Finally, because choices rest on the beliefs-values-norms-ethics-morality package (Chapter 1), helpers listen for these drivers and help clients see how they shape decisions and what their consequences are, rather than challenging the drivers themselves. Belinda and her husband had unknowingly adopted a parenting philosophy with consequences they did not want, and needed help discovering how to change.
sections.simple: Helping is about change, and change means choices. Inviting clients to challenge themselves is a stronger 'nudge' that helps them use their own resources. Good helping always mixes support and challenge, and challenge adds a 'discordant note' that helps clients see things differently. Egan prefers the softer word 'challenge' to 'confrontation'.
keyPoints: Chapters 6-7 are a form of choice architecture; self-challenge is a stronger nudge than in Chapter 5.
Balance evidence-based practice with centuries of practice-based evidence on self-improvement.
OR example: 60% in one survey found it hard to speak up; failure to challenge can be devastating.
All effective helping mixes support and challenge; either alone fails.
Martin, Trevino and Claiborn: discrepancy/discordance between helper and client views facilitates change.
'Challenge' is preferred to 'confrontation'; helpers help clients see their beliefs-values-norms drivers rather than attacking them.

sections.heading: The Goals of Challenging
sections.detailed:
Egan sets challenge within the ultimate goal of helping, which is life-enhancing, problem-managing outcomes for the client. The overall goal of challenging is to help clients do some reality testing and invest what they learn in creating a better future.

He states two related goals. The first is corrective: help clients challenge themselves to change the ways of thinking, expressing emotion and acting that keep them stuck in problem situations and stop them identifying and developing opportunities. Helping clients challenge self-defeating patterns of thinking, emotional expression and behaviour is especially important (Wei & Ku, 2007).

The second, parallel goal is more upbeat and concerns new perspectives and turning them into new action. Helpers become partners with clients in helping them challenge themselves to find possibilities in their problems; discover unused internal and external strengths and resources; invest those resources in the problems and opportunities of their lives; spell out possibilities for a better future; find ways of making that future real; and commit to the actions needed to make it happen.

Egan admits this sounds idealistic, but says it captures the spirit of the counsellor's role as a "catalyst for a better future". The two goals together mean that challenge is not only about finding faults; it is equally about unearthing strengths and opportunities and moving to action.
sections.simple: Challenge aims at reality testing that leads to a better future. One goal is to help clients drop self-defeating ways of thinking, feeling and acting. The other, more positive goal is to help them find possibilities, unused resources and commit to action, making the counsellor a 'catalyst for a better future'.
keyPoints: Ultimate goal of helping: life-enhancing, problem-managing outcomes.
Overall goal of challenging: reality testing invested in a better future.
Goal 1: challenge self-defeating thinking, emotional expression and behaviour (Wei & Ku).
Goal 2: find possibilities, unused resources, a better future and commitment to act.
Counsellor as 'catalyst for a better future'.

sections.heading: Target Areas of Self-Challenge
sections.detailed:
Because the two goals involve both correcting problems and building on strengths, some self-challenge involves self-criticism and some involves self-enhancement. Egan recommends Chang's (2007) edited book, which asks whether self-enhancement and self-criticism are good or bad, under what conditions, and what helpers should do about them, before committing to helping clients challenge themselves.

The guiding principle is that counsellors help clients challenge whatever stands in the way of understanding and managing problems or identifying and developing life-enhancing opportunities. The book lists the main targets of self-challenge:

1. Self-defeating mind-sets, such as prejudice.
2. Self-limiting internal behaviour, such as dysfunctional daydreaming.
3. Self-defeating expressions of feelings and emotions, such as flying off the handle.
4. Dysfunctional external behaviour, such as putting people down.
5. Distorted understanding of what the world is really like.
6. Discrepancies between thinking and acting.
7. Unused strengths and resources.
8. The predictable dishonesties of everyday life.

A ninth, final category, helping clients challenge themselves to participate fully in the helping process, is mentioned here and dealt with later. Each target is examined in its own sub-section with examples, and Egan finally shows (in the case of Minerva) that in practice these targets usually appear mixed together.
sections.simple: Self-challenge can be self-critical or self-enhancing. Helpers invite clients to challenge anything blocking problem management or opportunity development. Egan lists eight main targets, from self-defeating mind-sets to the everyday dishonesties, plus full participation in helping.
keyPoints: Self-challenge can involve self-criticism or self-enhancement (Chang, 2007).
Principle: challenge whatever blocks managing problems or developing opportunities.
Eight targets: mind-sets, internal behaviour, emotional expression, external behaviour, distorted view of the world, discrepancies, unused strengths, predictable dishonesties.
Ninth category: participating fully in the helping process (discussed later).

sections.heading: Target: Self-Defeating Mind-Sets
sections.detailed:
Mind-sets are more or less permanent states of mind: assumptions, attitudes, beliefs, values, biases, convictions, inclinations, norms, outlooks, points of view, unexamined perceptions of self, others and the world, preconceptions and prejudices. Carlos sees that Mara holds unexplored assumptions and norms rooted in her family culture, while her ambitions have been shaped by her US education; she is culturally a hybrid. It is not his place to take sides, but inviting her to explore these beliefs could help her decide about career and relationships, especially after the painful conversation with her father.

Mind-sets, productive or problematic, drive or at least leak into external behaviour. The principle: invite clients to turn outmoded, self-limiting mind-sets into self-enhancing, liberating perspectives that drive problem-managing and opportunity-developing action. Two kinds are illustrated.

Prejudices. Candace has trouble with a Jewish colleague and grew up believing a stereotype about Jews in business. The counsellor invites her to rethink it: if the colleague is treacherous, it is not because he is Jewish. Separating the person from the stereotype clarifies her thinking, but she now has two problems, the relationship and the prejudice, and must also see that in troubled relationships both parties usually contribute.

Self-limiting beliefs and assumptions. Albert Ellis developed rational-emotive behaviour therapy (REBT) and held that one of the most useful interventions is challenging clients' irrational, self-defeating beliefs, which people talk themselves into. The common beliefs he listed are: being liked and loved (I must always be loved and approved by significant others); being competent (I must be competent in all situations and talented in some important area); having one's own way (my plans must always work out); being hurt (wrongdoers, especially those who harm me, are evil and should be blamed and punished); being danger-free (I must be anxious about any danger and should not have to face it); being problemless (things should not go wrong, and if they do there should be quick, easy solutions); being a victim (others and outside forces cause my misery; nobody should take advantage of me); avoiding (it is easier to avoid difficulties than develop self-discipline); tyranny of the past (my past determines how I act and feel now); and passivity (I can be happy by being passive and uncommitted). When such beliefs are violated, people "catastrophize", seeing the event as awful; Ellis said this gets clients nowhere, the event is unfortunate but not the end of the world, and they can often act on it. Allison, a widow in her early 60s, has had a cancerous polyp removed with a good prognosis, yet catastrophizes about future tests; she is working from the "problemless" assumption and needs help to challenge it.

Sternberg (2002, 2003) described four fallacies that make smart people do stupid things: egocentrism (it is all about me), omniscience (knowing a lot about something becomes believing I know everything), omnipotence (I can do whatever I want) and invulnerability (I will not be caught, or can get out of any fix). These are visible in politics, business, entertainment and sport, but no one is exempt.

Riso, du Toit, Stein and Young (2007) edited a book on maladaptive cognitive schemas and core beliefs that characterise a range of disorders. The relatively new idea of schemas points not just to individual dysfunctional beliefs but to ingrained systems of thinking that cause trouble; helping clients identify and deal with them adds value.
sections.simple: Mind-sets are fairly permanent beliefs, attitudes and assumptions that drive behaviour. Helpers invite clients to swap self-limiting mind-sets, like prejudice or Ellis's irrational beliefs, for liberating ones. Sternberg's four fallacies and the idea of maladaptive schemas show how deeply such thinking can run.
keyPoints: Mind-sets = relatively permanent states of mind that drive or leak into behaviour.
Prejudice example: Candace separates her colleague from a stereotype.
Ellis (REBT): ten irrational beliefs, e.g. being loved, competent, problemless, a victim; catastrophizing gets clients nowhere.
Sternberg's four fallacies: egocentrism, omniscience, omnipotence, invulnerability.
Riso et al.: schemas are ingrained systems of thinking, not just single beliefs.

sections.heading: Target: Self-Limiting Internal Behavior
sections.detailed:
Egan argues that some forms of thinking are actually behaviours: things we can choose to do or not do. Internally we daydream, pray, ruminate, believe, identify problems, review opportunities, decide, plan, judge, question motives, approve and disapprove of ourselves and others, wonder, value, imagine, ponder, set standards, fashion norms, mull over, ignore, forgive and rehearse. These are internal or cognitive behaviours, not merely thoughts that happen to us. The helping principle: if clients are to replace self-limiting internal behaviour with more creative behaviour, they may need help. The ways internal behaviour can limit us are countless.

John daydreams of being a hero others admire; fantasy social success has replaced working for real success. The new perspective is that daydreaming is not bad in itself; it depends on how it is used. With a counsellor, John keeps daydreaming but redirects it to imagining a fuller social life, which yields practical strategies he starts trying.

Nadia, given a project, immediately hunts for reasons it will fail, and this internal behaviour spills into telling everyone it should be changed or shelved, annoying colleagues. Her supervisor helps her see that her instinct to take things apart reflects a lack of intellectual balance, and helps her build the habit of first asking what value the project adds and how she might improve it. She then critiques more constructively and is listened to.

Bella, depressed two years after her husband's death, says she stopped wearing black a year ago, "But..." The therapist responds, "But you're still wearing black inside?" The metaphor gives her the new perspective she needs; after a couple more sessions she begins to move beyond grieving. Similarly, Carlos notices that Mara sees herself as the "dutiful daughter" who puts her parents' needs before her own, which differs from being naturally generous while balancing one's own needs; exploring this mind-set could help her build a more fulfilling future.
sections.simple: Many kinds of thinking, like daydreaming, ruminating or judging, are internal behaviours we can choose. When they limit clients, helpers can help them redirect these behaviours. John redirects his daydreams, Nadia learns to look for value before criticising, and Bella realises she is 'still wearing black inside'.
keyPoints: Some thinking is behaviour: chosen internal or cognitive acts.
Principle: help clients replace self-limiting internal behaviour with creative internal behaviour.
John: daydreaming redirected to practical social goals.
Nadia: from automatic fault-finding to first seeing value; lacks intellectual balance.
Bella: metaphor 'wearing black inside' sparks a new perspective; Mara as 'dutiful daughter'.

sections.heading: Target: Self-Defeating Expressions of Feelings and Emotions
sections.detailed:
Managing emotions and how we express them is part of social-emotional intelligence. Some emotions are bottled up, some run on inside, and some are highly visible. Sheila becomes depressed when her boss ignores her good work and feels taken for granted, but puts on a good face at work. Ira, by contrast, rants about his "stupid" boss to anyone who listens; everyone except the boss knows where he stands.

Clients can be helped to face needless denial and bottling up of emotions, letting emotions run riot internally, and self-defeating ways of expressing emotion. Berking, Orth, Wupperman, Meier and Caspar (2008), in two studies, found that focusing on emotion-regulation skills may be important in preventing and treating affect-related mental-health problems. Egan raises the question of where people learn such skills while growing up.

Further examples: Arthur flies off the handle whenever anyone suggests a less acerbic style would help him and others; he needs help seeing the world as others see it. Cynthia lavishes praise on her two primary-school children because it makes her feel good, without asking what it does to them; she needs to learn that praise is not an unadulterated good. A counsellor helps Ken see that long periods of internet surfing trigger his depression; he needs to get out and interact with people to keep emotional balance. Mara has always presented herself as self-contained, and even when she broke down with Carlos she kept apologising for her tears and trying to control herself; emotional overcontrol may be part of her problem.
sections.simple: How we handle and show emotions is part of social-emotional intelligence. Clients can be helped with bottling up feelings, letting them run riot inside, or expressing them in self-defeating ways. Research by Berking and colleagues suggests emotion-regulation skills matter for preventing and treating mood-related problems.
keyPoints: Emotion management is part of social-emotional intelligence.
Three problems: needless denial/bottling up, emotions running riot inside, self-defeating expression.
Berking et al. (2008), two studies: emotion-regulation skills may matter for affect-related problems.
Examples: Sheila (bottles up), Ira (rants), Arthur (flies off the handle), Cynthia (over-praises), Ken (internet and depression).
Mara: emotional overcontrol may be part of the problem.

sections.heading: Target: Dysfunctional External Behavior
sections.detailed:
External behaviour is what people could see if they were looking, and for some clients it is the trouble. Achilles behaves towards women at work in ways others, including the courts, see as sexual harassment, while he thinks he is being "friendly". Jake is not an alcoholic but becomes mean and argumentative after a couple of drinks, believing he is helping others "get the point"; he needs to examine both his thinking and his acting. Clarence, self-doubting and over-cautious, is deferential to his manager, who reads this as lack of ambition but says nothing because she prefers an "obedient" employee; his behaviour keeps him in a job he hates.

Not doing something is also behaviour. Clients often fail to make choices and take actions that would help them. Clarence turns down skill updating and a promotion, telling himself he does not want to get in over his head; these self-defeating external behaviours rest on a self-defeating thought about himself. His manager notices but is content to keep a "hard-working drone".

Ryan has trouble with college classmates: he is aggressive, hogs conversations, tries to get his own way and criticises freely. A friend, after drinking, angrily calls him self-centred, arrogant and pushy. After a funk, he talks it through with a respected older dorm prefect, sees how self-defeating his style is, and works with a student-services counsellor on being proactive and assertive rather than aggressive. He takes an interpersonal-communication course, learns the value of dialogue, and applies it with classmates, at his part-time job and at home.
sections.simple: External behaviour is what others can see, and for some clients it is the core problem, like harassment or meanness after drinking. Failing to act is also behaviour, as when Clarence refuses opportunities. Ryan shows how a client can move from aggressive to assertive behaviour once he sees its cost.
keyPoints: External behaviour = what others could see if looking.
Examples: Achilles (harassment he calls 'friendly'), Jake (mean when drinking), Clarence (deference).
Not doing something is also a form of behaviour (Clarence refuses training and promotion).
Self-defeating external behaviour often rests on a self-defeating thought.
Ryan learns to be assertive rather than aggressive and to value dialogue.

sections.heading: Target: Distorted Understanding of the World
sections.detailed:
Clients' failure to see the world as it really is can keep them stuck in problems and stop them seeing opportunities. Parents may miss signs that their teenage son has started using drugs. If we are sometimes blind to others and their needs, often those closest to us, we are also blind to their attitudes toward us and to the impact of their behaviour on us.

Sandra interprets her husband's reduced interest in sex as a sign that he is "finally coming to his senses", and is shocked to learn by accident that he is having an affair. Egan stresses that everyone has areas of ignorance and naivety; clients' failure to understand their environment and its impact on them does not mean they are stupid. Like everyone, they simply fail to notice things that are hurting their lives. Helpers invite clients to test their picture of the world against reality.
sections.simple: Sometimes clients misread their world, like parents missing signs of drug use or Sandra misreading her husband's behaviour. This is not stupidity; everyone has blind areas. Helpers help clients check their view of reality.
keyPoints: Failure to see the world as it is keeps clients mired and blind to opportunities.
We are often blind to those closest to us and their impact on us.
Sandra misreads her husband's behaviour and is shocked by his affair.
Ignorance and naivety are universal and do not mean clients are stupid.

sections.heading: Target: Discrepancies
sections.simple: Discrepancies are gaps, for example between what clients say and do, or between their values and their behaviour. These gaps keep them stuck. In the Clarissa example, the counsellor gently points out her earlier enthusiasm, and she admits she has got used to being unemployed.
keyPoints: Six listed discrepancies: think/feel vs say; say vs do; self-view vs others' view; are vs want to be; goals vs achievements; values vs behaviour.
Examples: Tom, Minerva, George, Clarissa.
Clarissa: gentle, curious challenge reveals a 'culture of unemployment'.
Once out in the open, a discrepancy becomes something to work on together.

sections.heading: Target: Unused Strengths and Resources
sections.detailed:
Self-challenge should focus not only on problems but on the "possible self" each client is. Helping clients get in touch with unexploited opportunities and unused or underused strengths and resources (Aspinwall & Staudinger, 2003; Tedeschi & Kilmer, 2005) adds great value. Some resources are client-based, such as unused talents and abilities; some are external, such as failing to identify and use social support. Therapists help clients ask: what unused strengths do I have, and how can I unleash and marshal internal and external resources? Everyone has resources that need to be mined.

Strengths are buried even in dysfunctional behaviour. Driscoll (1984) pointed out that helpers can show clients that even their "irrationalities" can be a source of strength. Instead of forcing clients to see how stupidly they think and act, therapists can help them find the logic embedded in seemingly dysfunctional ideas and behaviour, and then use that logic as a resource to manage problems rather than perpetuate them. Egan describes a psychiatrist friend who helped a client see the "beauty" of an elaborate self-defence system he had built to cocoon himself from life, showing him how inventive and powerful it was, so that the same inventiveness could be redirected.
sections.simple: Challenge is also about strengths, not only problems. Helpers help clients find unused internal talents and external resources like social support. Driscoll showed that even 'irrational' behaviour contains logic and strength that can be turned to good use.
keyPoints: Focus on the 'possible self', not just problems.
Resources are internal (talents, abilities) and external (social support).
Key questions: what unused strengths do I have; how can I marshal my resources?
Driscoll (1984): even 'irrationalities' contain logic that can be a strength.
Psychiatrist example: appreciating the inventiveness of a self-defence system.

sections.heading: Target: The Predictable Dishonesties of Everyday Life
sections.detailed:
The "predictable dishonesties of life" are the distortions, evasions, games, tricks, excuse making and smoke screens that keep clients, and all of us, stuck. Everyone has ways of defending against themselves, others and the world. These little dishonesties are two-edged: a lie may help me cope with an unexpected difficulty but carries a price, especially if it becomes a preferred coping strategy; blaming others saves face but damages relationships and blocks self-responsibility. The purpose of challenging them, whether in sessions or as wider patterns, is not to strip clients of their defences, which could sometimes be dangerous, but to help them cope more creatively with their inner and outer worlds.

Distortions. Some clients would rather not see the world as it is because it is too painful or demanding, so they distort it in self-serving ways. Arnie fears his supervisor and sees her as aloof, though she is caring; he works out of past fears rather than present reality. Edna casts her counsellor in a divine role and makes unwarranted demands. Nancy treats getting her own way as the test of whether friends like her. With Nancy, who is in conflict with her husband Milan over their 12-year-old son Jan cycling to school, the counsellor's tentative remark that Milan surely cares about Jan removes the implied distortion that only she cares. Probing their decision-making then suggests the issue is as much about power and getting her own way as about parenting; Nancy has her own "little dishonesties".

Games, tricks and smoke screens. Clients who are comfortable with and profit from their delusions will try to keep them; if rewarded for playing games inside or outside counselling, they continue a game approach to life (Berne, 1964). Kennard plays "Yes, but...": he asks for recommendations on controlling anger and then shows why each will not work, and when challenged says counsellors are not supposed to tell clients what to do; a savvier helper would have spotted this earlier. Dora appears helpless with friends, then resents them for treating her like a child; her counsellor invites her to examine this routine. Fearful clients lay smoke screens and use communication in order not to communicate, so helpers should create an atmosphere that discourages games.

Excuses. Snyder, Higgins and Stucky (1983) studied excuse making in depth; it is universal and part of everyday life (also Halleck; Higginson; Snyder & Higgins; Yun). Like games and distortions it has positive uses, and there is no reason to want a world without myths, but excuses contribute heavily to avoiding life's problems. People excuse why they did something bad, why they did not do something good, and why they cannot do what they need to. Roberto has made "benign" attempts to sabotage his wife Maria's career "for her own good" so she would not get hurt in the Anglo world. Before marriage he said he would enjoy a wife with a "pioneer" spirit; now she has a career, earns more than him, and he feels he is losing face, belittled and forced into an overly "democratic" marriage. The counsellor helps him explore the alternative hypothesis that he is not ready for the changes her career demands. Egan concludes that skilled helpers are caring and empathic but do not let themselves be conned, because that helps no one.
sections.simple: Everyone uses small dishonesties like distortions, games and excuses to protect themselves, but they keep us stuck. The aim of challenging them is not to strip away defences but to help clients cope more creatively. Skilled helpers are caring but do not let themselves be conned.
keyPoints: Dishonesties = distortions, evasions, games, tricks, excuses, smoke screens; they are two-edged swords.
Aim: not to strip defences (could be dangerous) but help clients cope more creatively.
Distortions are self-serving (Arnie, Edna, Nancy).
Games (Berne): Kennard's 'Yes, but...', Dora's helplessness; create an atmosphere that discourages games.
Excuses (Snyder, Higgins & Stucky): universal, have uses, but help avoid problems (Roberto).
Skilled helpers are empathic but not conned.

sections.heading: Mixed Targets and the ACT Caution
sections.detailed:
In practice the targets of challenge are mixed together. Minerva is depressed by her lack of a social life. Because of a few traumatic past experiences she believes the world is full of dishonest people (self-limiting mind-set). She views each new person as guilty until proved innocent (internal behaviour needing reform). Always on guard, she seems cold and indifferent (poor management of feelings and emotions). She is defensive and questions others' intentions (external behaviour needing change). She expects initial trust from others while not giving it herself (a discrepancy). She looks for flaws and pounces on them (a self-defeating game). She does not notice that even close friends are becoming uncomfortable (failure to see the world as it is). In sessions she stays guarded and slow to share (inadequate participation). Worse, she has no idea she is doing all this, which leads into the topic of blind spots.

The section ends with a caution from Steven Hayes about the pervasiveness of self-defeating thoughts and emotions. In acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), Hayes invites clients to step out of their endless war with "bad" thoughts and feelings: rather than spending energy avoiding or confronting them, clients embrace and defuse them with respectful attention, changing their relationship to them. Instead of disputing negative thoughts, clients watch them mindfully at enough distance to realise, in a felt and not just intellectual way, that they are just thoughts; instead of getting rid of sadness, they learn how it feels in the body and how it tugs at behaviour, and that they can carry sorrow while living the life they want.

Then Hayes helps clients decide what they want to live for and, with that sense of purpose, how they want to live. Befriending troublesome thoughts clears the way for the real work of life, helping clients turn a life lived in the present into a life worth living. ACT is therefore mildly directive: therapists help clients place demands on themselves to rebuild their lives. Hayes has written extensively on the research behind it.
sections.simple: Real clients show several targets at once: Minerva has a distrustful mind-set, cold emotions, defensive behaviour, a discrepancy, a game and poor participation, without realising it. Hayes's ACT warns against endless war with bad thoughts: accept and defuse them mindfully, then commit to a purposeful life.
keyPoints: Targets are usually mixed: Minerva illustrates all of them, including inadequate participation.
Minerva is unaware of her pattern, leading into blind spots.
Hayes's ACT: stop warring with 'bad' thoughts and feelings; embrace and defuse them with respectful attention.
Clients learn that thoughts are just thoughts and they can carry sorrow while living fully.
ACT then clarifies purpose; it is mildly directive.

sections.heading: Inviting Clients to Challenge the Blind Spots at the Root of Dysfunctional Thinking, Emotional Expression, and Behavior
sections.detailed:
So far the chapter has dealt with what needs challenging, the content. Egan now adds the client's degree of awareness of self-limiting thinking, emotional expression and behaviour. Like everyone, clients do not always realise, or fully realise, how they limit themselves; they have blind spots. Blind spots are part of the human condition: things we fail to see or choose to ignore that keep us from identifying and managing problems or identifying and developing opportunities.

Van Hecke (2007) describes ten common blind spots that get people into trouble: failure to think things through; always having the right answers; failure to pick up cues and clues and notice what is going on; lack of self-awareness; failure to explore one's biases; seeing the world through rigid categories; jumping to conclusions; failure to check things out; seeing coincidences as causes; and failure to see the big picture and put things in context. She notes that we readily see others' blind spots and the stupidities they cause, but stay ignorant of our own; what we grasp seems so obvious that we cannot understand how others miss it.

So clients may be perceptive about others yet need help sharpening their perception of themselves. Blind spots are obstacles to effective decision making. Egan then describes the different kinds, or "flavours", of blind spots: lack of awareness, failure to think things through, self-deception, choosing to stay in the dark, and knowing but not caring or failing to see consequences.
sections.simple: Beyond what to challenge, helpers must consider how aware clients are of their self-limiting patterns. Blind spots are things we fail to see or choose to ignore, and everyone has them. Van Hecke lists ten common ones; we spot others' blind spots easily but miss our own.
keyPoints: Shift from content of challenge to client's degree of awareness.
Blind spots: things we fail to see or choose to ignore that block problem management and opportunity development.
Van Hecke's ten blind spots, e.g. jumping to conclusions, rigid categories, seeing coincidences as causes.
We see others' blind spots but not our own.
Blind spots obstruct effective decision making.

sections.heading: Lack of Awareness
sections.detailed:
Some blind spots seem unintentional and others self-inflicted, but both block change. Some things clients simply are not aware of, and becoming aware helps them know themselves and cope with problems and opportunities.

Serge, raised in a family that prized modesty and humility, was surprised when a self-help group member called him talented; he had never seen himself as talented, creative or resourceful and did not realise how this narrowed his life. His mind-set blocked change. Katya, always upbeat, "exuded sunshine", but did not realise that her exuberance was sometimes inappropriate because it kept her from facing problems squarely; a colleague felt it needed a dose of reality. Her friend Mia thought her emotional outbursts were part of a punchy style, unaware that colleagues sometimes wanted to strangle her. Casper did not know his style was acerbic; he saw himself as assertive and logical, while others saw pushiness and stubbornness and avoided him, so his social life suffered.

"Simple unawareness" is elastic and comes in degrees. At one end is simple ignorance ("he doesn't have a clue"); at the other the ignorance is not so simple, as when Mia says Casper probably has some idea he rubs people the wrong way and is not totally in the dark. Note that unawareness can concern strengths (Serge) as well as weaknesses (Katya, Mia, Casper).
sections.simple: Some blind spots are simply things clients do not know about themselves, such as unrecognised talents or an off-putting style. Unawareness comes in degrees, from having no clue to half knowing. Becoming aware helps clients change.
keyPoints: Blind spots may be unintentional or self-inflicted; both block change.
Serge: unaware of his talents because of family values of modesty.
Katya, Mia, Casper: unaware of how their style affects others.
Simple unawareness is elastic: from no clue to partial awareness.

sections.heading: Failure to Think Things Through
sections.detailed:
A very common human experience is exploring problems, examining opportunities, searching for possibilities or planning in an incomplete, haphazard way, and then basing decisions on that flawed reasoning.

Kim and Lea, long-time neighbours and friends, have both lost sons in Iraq. Kim thinks the war was a mistake and blames the politicians; Lea believes it was essential and her son died for a just cause. Their emotionally charged convictions leave neither any feeling for the other's view, and they are willing to destroy their friendship, which neither son would have wanted. Here strong convictions intensified by emotion stop them thinking things through; in other cases habit, laziness or thoughtlessness is the cause. Counsellors who challenge clients and help them think key issues through provide an invaluable service.

Failure to explore the short- and long-term consequences of a dysfunctional pattern is also very common. Clancy knew he could get into trouble with classmates who lost all limits when out together ("group think" and "group act"). Ignoring his mother's warnings, he went out of town with them over a holiday weekend, got drunk, trashed a hotel, pushed a police officer, ended up in hospital, received two years' probation and was expelled from his private school. After one or two more incidents and help from a counsellor familiar with such stories, he rebuilt his life. Egan asks whether failing to see consequences ruined his life or taught him an invaluable lesson.
sections.simple: People often think through problems and plans in a haphazard way and then act on poor reasoning. Strong emotional convictions, habit or laziness can block clear thinking, as with Kim and Lea. Failing to foresee consequences, as Clancy did, can wreck a life, so helping clients think things through is invaluable.
keyPoints: Haphazard exploration and planning leads to decisions based on flawed reasoning.
Kim and Lea: emotion-charged convictions block thinking things through.
Other causes: habit, laziness, thoughtlessness.
Failure to foresee short- and long-term consequences (Clancy).
Helping clients think key issues through is an invaluable service.

sections.heading: Self-Deception
sections.detailed:
Egan asks where lack of awareness or failure to think things through ends and self-deception begins. There are things clients would rather not know, because knowing would challenge them to change, so they stay in the dark.

Goleman, well known for writing on social and emotional intelligence, earlier wrote Vital Lies, Simple Truths (1985) on the psychology of self-deception and how pervasive it is. Egan notes that self-deception and the social-emotional maturity described in Goleman's Emotional Intelligence are incompatible.

Yet, as Eduardo Giannetti (1997) argues in Lies We Live By: The Art of Self-Deception, self-deception is everywhere; he marvels at how we manage to believe what we do not believe and lie to ourselves while believing the lie. Stan, though engaged, thought he could get away with flirting, excusing it as natural for a man. His fiancée found it insulting and called off the wedding, and Stan painfully discovered the price of his self-deception.
sections.simple: Self-deception is when clients avoid knowing something because knowing it would push them to change. Goleman and Giannetti show how common it is, and it clashes with emotional maturity. Stan's flirting cost him his engagement.
keyPoints: Self-deception: not wanting to know because knowing would demand change.
Goleman, Vital Lies, Simple Truths (1985): self-deception is pervasive.
Self-deception is incompatible with emotional-intelligence maturity.
Giannetti (1997), Lies We Live By: self-deception is ubiquitous.
Stan's excuse for flirting cost him his engagement.

sections.heading: Choosing to Stay in the Dark
sections.detailed:
Choosing to stay in the dark is common: it is like saying "I could find out, but I don't want to, at least not yet." Heffernan (2011) calls this "willful blindness". She argues that we make ourselves powerless when we choose not to know but give ourselves hope when we insist on looking; precisely because willful blindness is willed, the product of experience, knowledge, thinking, neurons and neuroses, we have the capacity to change it.

Many people avoid thinking about physical symptoms such as gut pain, which can be life-threatening, because finding out might be uncomfortable or intolerable. Clients, like everyone, often choose to stay in the dark. Ilia, just released from jail, knows she should understand her probation conditions but chooses not to, claiming nobody explained them, and pushes out of mind the risk of returning to jail. Egan adds a practical point for helpers: when clients are vague or evasive with helpers, they may also be hiding something from themselves that would hurt to know more fully.
sections.simple: Sometimes clients could find something out but choose not to, which Heffernan calls 'willful blindness'. Because it is chosen, it can also be changed. Vagueness or evasiveness in sessions can be a sign that clients are hiding something from themselves.
keyPoints: Choosing to stay in the dark: 'I could find out but don't want to'.
Heffernan (2011): willful blindness; because it is willed, it can be changed.
Avoiding medical symptoms can be life-threatening.
Ilia chooses not to understand her probation conditions.
Client vagueness/evasiveness may signal self-concealment.

sections.heading: Knowing, Not Caring, and Failing to See Consequences
sections.detailed:
Sometimes clients know that their thinking, emotional expression and actions are getting or keeping them in trouble, but do not seem to care. Egan uses "blind spot" in an extended sense here, because they do not fully appreciate how far they are choosing their own misery or the consequences of not caring (think of Clancy). Tanel knows that nagging his wife to get a job while their two children are young annoys her, but continues ("I can't help it"); he focuses on her reluctance rather than the resentment building in her. Egan leaves the case unresolved and asks the reader how they would proceed.

Egan admits "blind spot" is elastic as used here: we are unaware, deceive ourselves, do not want to know, ignore, do not care, or know but not fully understand implications and consequences. Still it is a good term with great face validity; people immediately know what it means. Helping clients deal with blind spots is one of the most important things a helper can do.

Lester illustrates levels. If he has a prejudice and does not advert to it, he has a blind spot. If he adverts to it only vaguely, he is keeping himself in the dark. If he knows and, asked, says everyone he knows is like that, he does not care and fails to explore the human meaning of prejudice; he is prejudiced, knows it, fosters it and lets it shape how he treats people, the full dysfunctional package. Bernice, by contrast, starts unaware, becomes aware, tries to remove the prejudice from her mental furniture, refuses to act on it and learns about herself and the world; she turns a problem into an opportunity. Helping with blind spots can prevent damage, limit damage already done and turn problems into opportunities.

Box 6.1, "Questions to Uncover Blind Spots", lists questions clients can be helped to ask themselves to develop new perspectives and change internal and external behaviour: What problems am I avoiding? What opportunities am I ignoring? What's really going on? What am I overlooking? What do I refuse to see? What don't I want to do? What unverified assumptions am I making? What am I failing to factor in? How am I being dishonest with myself? What's underneath the rocks? If others were honest with me, what would they tell me? Egan notes that new perspectives are often called insights in therapy, and that insight has a long and somewhat problematic history in the helping professions.
sections.simple: Some clients know their behaviour causes trouble but do not care or do not see the consequences, like Tanel nagging his wife. 'Blind spot' is a loose but useful term covering many kinds of not-seeing. Lester shows the full dysfunctional package; Bernice turns her prejudice into growth. Box 6.1 gives self-questions to uncover blind spots.
keyPoints: Knowing but not caring, or not seeing consequences, is a blind spot in an extended sense (Tanel).
'Blind spot' is elastic but has great face validity.
Lester: blind spot -> keeping self in dark -> not caring = full dysfunctional package.
Bernice turns prejudice into an opportunity; dealing with blind spots prevents/limits damage.
Box 6.1: eleven questions to uncover blind spots; new perspectives are often called insights.

sections.heading: Specific Skills for Helping Clients Challenge Their Blind Spots and Move to New Perspectives
sections.detailed:
Self-challenge aims at understanding that leads to constructive change. It is a disservice to help clients only identify and explore their blind spots. The upbeat part is helping them transform blind spots into new perspectives and translate these into more constructive internal and external behaviour.

Egan lists many upbeat names for this process: seeing things more clearly, getting the picture, getting insights, developing new perspectives, spelling out implications, transforming perceptions, new frames of reference, looking for meaning, shifting perceptions, seeing the bigger picture, different angles, seeing things in context, context breaking, rethinking, getting a more objective view, interpreting, overcoming blind spots, second-level learning, double-loop learning (Argyris, 1999), thinking creatively, reconceptualising, discovering, having an "ah-ha" experience, developing a new outlook, questioning assumptions, getting rid of distortions, relabelling and making connections. Terms such as "frame breaking", "frame bending" and "reframing" are also used. All imply some cognitive restructuring needed to manage problems and opportunities. Although sometimes painful, new perspectives tend to be prized by clients in the end.

One way to help clients challenge internal and external actions is to help them explore consequences. Roberto calls his mild sabotage of Maria's career "delaying tactics". The helper proposes reviewing what impact the tactics have had on Maria and the marriage and where they are likely to lead; Roberto admits she has become even more stubborn, and discovers his sabotage works against him and endangers the marriage.

Effective helpers assume clients have the resources to see themselves and their world less distortedly and to act on what they see. In Alcoholics Anonymous language, they help clients move from "stinkin' thinkin'" to healthy thinking, from "stinkin'" emoting to constructive emotional expression, and from dysfunctional to healthy behaviour. Carla, facing menopause, holds the outdated view that it is a "deficiency disease"; without minimising her discomfort, a counsellor helps her see it as a natural developmental stage that ends one phase but opens new possibilities, and looking forward rather than back helps her greatly.

Invitations to self-challenge lie on a continuum from indirect to direct. Egan starts with three indirect approaches: advanced empathy (identifying and sharing the message behind the message), information sharing and helper self-disclosure. He then turns to more direct approaches: suggestions and recommendations, confrontation, and finally encouragement.
sections.simple: It is not enough to spot blind spots; helpers must help clients turn them into new perspectives and new behaviour. This goes by many names, such as reframing, insight or double-loop learning. Exploring consequences and reframing (as with Roberto and Carla) are examples. The skills run from indirect (advanced empathy, information, self-disclosure) to direct (suggestions, confrontation) plus encouragement.
keyPoints: Goal: transform blind spots into new perspectives and new behaviour.
Many names: insight, reframing, frame breaking, double-loop learning (Argyris), etc.; all imply cognitive restructuring.
Exploring consequences (Roberto's 'delaying tactics').
From 'stinkin' thinkin'' (AA) to healthy thinking; Carla reframes menopause.
Indirect skills: advanced empathy, information sharing, self-disclosure; direct: suggestions, confrontation; plus encouragement.

sections.heading: Advanced Empathy: Capturing the Fuller Message or the Message Behind the Message
sections.detailed:
Egan recalls Carl Rogers's point (from Chapter 5) that empathy sometimes involves sensing meanings the client is scarcely aware of. This fuller message, or message behind the message, is what Egan calls advanced empathy when the helper shares it. Gordon gets angry talking about his ex-wife, but the helper also hears hurt, which Gordon finds harder to discuss.

Basic empathy, if accurate, is recognised immediately ("Yes, that's what I meant"). Advanced empathy digs deeper into more covert messages, so clients may not recognise themselves at once and may feel some disequilibrium; that is what makes it a form of challenge, inviting a closer look at oneself. When the helper tells Gordon he obviously gets steamed but seems to have a bit of hurt mixed in, Gordon looks down, pauses and admits she can still get to him, which broadens and deepens the discussion.

Helpers can ask themselves: What is this person only half saying? What is he or she hinting at? What is being said in a confused way? What covert message lies behind the explicit one? Advanced empathy focuses on what the client is actually saying or expressing, however tentatively or confusedly; it is not interpretation and not an attempt to "psych the client out". In skilled hands it targets not only problems but unused opportunities and resources buried and forgotten in clients.

The soldier example: a hardworking soldier who served in Iraq and Afghanistan keeps being passed over for promotion and says he is not as flashy as others but just as substantial. Chaplain A responds with basic empathy (it feels unfair), and the soldier retreats into resignation and silence. Chaplain B acknowledges the depression of being passed by, then picks up the phrase "not as flashy" and wonders whether something in his style makes him easy to overlook. The soldier realises he is so unassuming he might get lost in the shuffle and has never thought of selling himself. Drawing on context, the discussion and the client's manner and tone, Chaplain B picked up a theme stated in passing, and they go on to discuss how he might market himself consistently with his values.

Advanced empathy takes several forms, discussed next: helping clients make the implied explicit, identify themes, make missing connections, and sharing educated hunches.
sections.simple: Advanced empathy means sensing and sharing the deeper message behind what the client says, such as hurt beneath anger. Because clients may not recognise it immediately, it challenges them to look closer. It sticks to what the client is actually expressing, not the helper's theories, and can reveal strengths as well as problems.
keyPoints: Rooted in Rogers: sensing meanings the client is scarcely aware of.
Basic empathy is recognised immediately; advanced empathy may cause mild disequilibrium, hence challenge.
Self-questions: what is only half said, hinted at, said confusedly, the covert message?
Not interpretation or 'psyching out'; based on what the client expresses.
Chaplain A (basic) vs Chaplain B (picks up 'not as flashy' theme).

sections.heading: Advanced Empathy Form: Help Clients Make the Implied Explicit
sections.detailed:
The most basic form of advanced empathy helps clients give fuller expression to what they are implying rather than saying directly. A recently divorced client discusses contacting his ex-wife but with little enthusiasm, hesitantly saying there is nothing wrong with calling to see how she is.

Counselor A gives a basic-empathy response, agreeing there is nothing wrong with taking the initiative since he wants to know she is okay. The client drearily agrees and does not move on. This might have suited an earlier stage but misses the mark now.

Counselor B notes that, unless she is mistaken, she does not hear much enthusiasm in his voice. The client admits he does not want to talk to her; he feels guilty about the divorce and her being alone, and is really trying to take care of her again, which was one reason they divorced: he needed to take care of her and she let him though she resented it. Asked what a better approach would be, he says they both need to get on with their lives, neither is helpless, and, brightening, mentions a business idea he has been considering with a friend.

Counselor B based her response on the whole context of his story, not just the last remark, and it hit the mark. Egan stresses that, as with basic empathy, there is no such thing as a good advanced highlight in itself; the test is whether it helps the client clarify the issue so that he or she begins to see the need to act differently.
sections.simple: The simplest form of advanced empathy helps clients say openly what they are only implying. In the divorce example, noticing the client's lack of enthusiasm leads him to admit guilt and a pattern of caretaking, and then to talk about a new opportunity. A response is good only if it helps the client move forward.
keyPoints: Most basic form: help clients express fully what they imply.
Counselor A (basic empathy) misses the mark; client stalls.
Counselor B notices lack of enthusiasm, drawing on the whole context.
Client reveals guilt and caretaking pattern, then a new opportunity.
No highlight is good in itself; judge by whether it helps the client see the need to act.

sections.heading: Advanced Empathy Form: Help Clients Identify Themes in Their Stories
sections.detailed:
When clients tell their stories, themes often emerge. Thematic material may concern feelings (hurt, depression, anxiety), thoughts (constantly ruminating over a past mistake), behaviour (controlling others, avoiding intimacy, blaming others, overwork), experiences (being a victim, seduced, punished, ignored, picked on) or combinations. Once the helper sees a self-defeating theme or pattern, he or she can share the perception and help the client check it out.

Egan's example is a supervision session. A counselling-psychology trainee has seen four clients for the third time and feels he is going round in circles with some. He thinks he has been very good at listening and sharing highlights, which keeps clients talking, but there is no movement. They listen to a tape, and he realises it is all basic empathy with a few "uh-huhs"; he had thought he was being pushy but is as far from pushy as possible. The supervisor asks what is missing: very few probes, no summaries and no mild invitations to self-challenge. After a 15-minute role play in which the trainee mixes probes with basic highlights, the session is quite different. Asked how close he got to challenging, he admits he did not get there at all; he sees probes as invitations to self-challenge, and recognises that the thread running through his work is "playing it safe" because he is afraid of damaging clients. The supervisor has helped him surface the theme of fear of being pushy, which explains his safe behaviour.
sections.simple: Advanced empathy can help clients spot recurring themes in their stories, such as avoiding intimacy or always blaming others. The helper shares the pattern tentatively and lets the client check it. A supervisor helps a trainee see his theme of 'playing it safe' out of fear of being pushy.
keyPoints: Themes may concern feelings, thoughts, behaviours, experiences, or combinations.
Share a perceived self-defeating theme and help the client check it out.
Trainee: all basic empathy, few probes, no summaries or challenge.
Underlying theme: fear of being pushy -> 'playing it safe'.

sections.heading: Advanced Empathy Form: Help Clients Make Connections That May Be Missing
sections.detailed:
Clients often tell their stories, experiences, thoughts, behaviours and emotions in a hit-or-miss way. The counsellor's job is to help them make the connections that provide insights or perspectives enabling them to move forward.

Examples: Chu Hua's counsellor helps her see that she struggles to develop strategies because she is only half-heartedly committed to her goals, so they revisit how realistic the goals are. Owen says he has a "problem with" pornography, avoids the word "addiction", and offers excuses; the therapist summarises and adds that she is not sure whether he is saying it is really his wife who has the problem. Owen admits he would be furious if roles were reversed, the therapist suggests starting over, and wiping the slate clean lets him explore his addiction. A therapist helps Joanna link her ingratiating style to her inability to influence colleagues. A supervisor helps Dieter, working for an NGO on poverty in Kenya, see that his anxiety with tribal leaders stems from perfectionist standards out of place in Kenyan culture.

The extended case is John, who works full time, is finishing his degree and whose father has had a stroke. He is increasingly tired and edgy and wonders if it is physical. The counsellor lists the stresses; John insists juggling is what he is good at. When asked what is different besides his dad's illness, John slowly identifies the squabbling at family meetings, which he keeps thinking about at work and while writing papers. He had expected the family to rally together. The connection: John handles normal stress well, but the "family stuff" acts as a multiplier, and they go on to discuss family dynamics and how he can cope.
sections.simple: Clients often tell their stories in bits, without linking them. Helpers help them connect the pieces, for example linking half-hearted commitment to weak strategies, or tiredness to family squabbling. These connections give insight that lets clients move forward.
keyPoints: Clients tell stories hit-or-miss; helpers help connect the pieces.
Chu Hua: weak strategies linked to half-hearted goal commitment.
Owen: summary plus tentative challenge leads him to own his porn addiction.
Joanna (ingratiating style) and Dieter (perfectionism out of place in Kenyan culture).
John: family squabbling acts as a stress multiplier.

sections.heading: Advanced Empathy Form: Share Educated Hunches Based on Empathic Understanding
sections.detailed:
As helpers listen, process and put things in context, they naturally form hunches about the message or story behind the story, and can share those likely to add value. The more mature, socially competent and experienced the helper, the more "educated" the hunches become. Egan lists six purposes, each with an example:

1. Helping clients see the bigger picture. A perfectionist client calls his brother-in-law a guy who can never get anything right; the counsellor wonders whether his perfectionism is "spreading", so that everyone else should be perfect too. They discuss its effect on his social life.
2. Helping clients go a bit deeper. To a client let down by a friend, the counsellor suggests she may feel more than disappointed, perhaps betrayed; since she has been avoiding the friend, "betrayal" rings truer and she contacts the depth of her feelings.
3. Helping clients see implications and draw conclusions. A manager stitches together a team member's tentative reservations and suggests she may be saying the project was ill-advised and should be shut down, inviting discussion.
4. Helping clients open up areas they are only hinting at. A school counsellor tells a high-school senior that he keeps raising sexual matters without pursuing them, guessing the area is important but sensitive.
5. Helping clients see things they may be overlooking. A man with perhaps six months to live, unmarried with no will and self-described as financially lazy, is told his laziness may have spread: he has no health power of attorney, so doctors may decide how he dies. He begins rethinking how he wants to die and even discusses giving his money to a good cause.
6. Helping clients own their stories, that is, take fuller ownership of partly owned experiences, behaviours, feelings, views and decisions. To a woman in painful rehabilitation after a car accident, the counsellor says she sounds as if she has already decided to quit, or perhaps that overstates it. She admits she has been afraid to discuss quitting; they explore her wish and dread of giving up, and, learning she has never told staff about the pain, plan direct conversations with them.

Guidelines: hunches must be based on understanding of the client; if asked "What makes you think that?", the helper should be able to point to the experiential and behavioural clues behind them. Empathy is not a licence to draw inferences at will from the client's history, nor to load clients with interpretations rooted more in the helper's favourite theories than in the client's reality. Constructive advanced empathy requires the helper's emotional intelligence and social competence.
sections.simple: Experienced helpers form hunches about the story behind the story and share them tentatively. Hunches can show the bigger picture, deepen feelings, draw out implications, open up hinted topics, reveal what is overlooked and help clients own their stories. They must rest on real clues from the client, not on the helper's pet theories.
keyPoints: Hunches grow more 'educated' with maturity, social competence and experience.
Six uses: bigger picture, go deeper, implications/conclusions, open up, see what is overlooked, own the story.
Examples: perfectionism 'spreading', 'betrayed' not just 'let down', no power of attorney, 'already decided to quit'.
Be able to name the clues behind a hunch.
Not a licence for free inference or theory-driven interpretation; needs emotional intelligence.

sections.heading: Information Sharing
sections.detailed:
Clients sometimes cannot explore problems fully, set goals or act because they lack information. Information can help at any stage: early on, knowing they are not the first to face a problem; later, clarifying possibilities and setting goals; in implementation, information about common obstacles helps them cope and persevere.

Information sharing is classed as a challenging skill because it helps clients develop new perspectives on their problems or shows them how to act. It includes both providing new information and correcting misinformation. Sometimes it is confirming and supportive: a parent blaming himself or herself after a newborn's death may feel some relief on learning the earmarks of sudden infant death syndrome; the information does not solve the problem, but the new perspective helps with self-blame.

New perspectives can be both comforting and painful. Adrian, a hardworking student of modest intellectual means, was rejected by every graduate psychology programme he applied to. He believed most college students went to graduate school because his close friends did. The counsellor shared statistics on the "educational pyramid", the shrinking percentage of students at each higher level. Adrian realised that finishing college already placed him in an elite group and learned how competitive the programmes were. This was a relief, but he was then disconcerted by the sudden need to face the world of work.

Information is especially useful when lack of accurate information is a main cause of a problem or is making it worse. In some medical settings doctors team with counsellors to deliver hard messages and information for difficult decisions. Doug, a 71-year-old accountant diagnosed with prostate cancer, hears the doctor lay out all options, including doing nothing, with their pros and cons; a counsellor then helps him cope, process the information and start deciding.

Cautions for giving information: when it is challenging or shocking, be tactful and help the client handle the disequilibrium; do not overwhelm the client; make sure it is clear and relevant to the problem; do not let the client leave with a misunderstanding; be supportive and help the client process it; and do not confuse information giving with advice giving. Professional guidance is not telling clients what to do; neither doctor nor counsellor tells Doug which treatment to choose, but he needs help with the burden of choosing.
sections.simple: Clients sometimes lack information, and giving it, or correcting misinformation, can create new perspectives. It can be comforting (SIDS facts easing guilt) or both relieving and painful (Adrian and the educational pyramid). Helpers must be tactful, clear, relevant and supportive, and must not turn information into advice.
keyPoints: Information helps at every stage: early, goal setting, implementation.
A challenging skill: it creates new perspectives or shows how to act; includes correcting misinformation.
SIDS example: information eases self-blame; Adrian: educational pyramid.
Especially useful when lack of information causes or worsens the problem; Doug's cancer decision.
Cautions: tact, don't overwhelm, clear and relevant, check understanding, be supportive, don't confuse with advice.

sections.heading: Helper Self-Disclosure
sections.detailed:
Another route to client self-challenge is the helper's ability and willingness to share some of his or her own experiences, thoughts, behaviours and feelings. The topic has been explored thoroughly (Barnett; Farber; Forrest; Henretty & Levitt; Kelly & Rodriguez; Myers & Hayes; Veach; Yeh & Hayes; Zur et al.), but there is no single voice on its value, limits and dangers.

In one sense counsellors cannot avoid disclosing themselves: Strong and Claiborne (1982) note that counsellors communicate their characteristics in every look, movement, emotional response, sound and word. This indirect disclosure goes on constantly, so effective helpers track and manage the impressions they make.

The chapter's concern is direct self-disclosure, where research is mixed and even contradictory. Henretty and Levitt (2010), in one of the most detailed reviews, say the problem begins with definition: multiple definitions make meaningful comparison across studies difficult if not impossible. Some studies find helper disclosure frightens clients, makes helpers seem less well adjusted, or burdens clients; others find clients appreciate it and see disclosing helpers as "down-to-earth" and "honest".

Direct self-disclosure can serve as modelling. Self-help groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous and drug treatment programmes use it extensively, and some say it is most appropriate there. It shows newcomers what to talk about and gives them courage, signalling that they can speak without being judged or hurt. Beth, a former substance abuser now counselling in the agency that helped her, freely shares her experience of using and her agonising journey to freedom whenever she thinks it will help. Other things being equal, counsellors who have struggled with addiction often make excellent helpers in such programmes because they know the games clients play from the inside; sharing is central to their style and accepted by clients, and it helps clients develop new perspectives and possibilities for action. It puts pressure on clients to talk more openly or in a more focused way.

Helper self-disclosure is challenging for at least two reasons. First, it is a form of intimacy, which some clients find hard to handle, so helpers must know precisely why they are disclosing. Second, its indirect message is "You can do it, too", since disclosures, even of past failures, usually centre on problems overcome or opportunities seized. Done well, such disclosure can be very encouraging.

Rick, counselling Tim (a troubled adolescent who fell in with the wrong crowd, had police trouble and strained relations with his parents), shares that he was expelled for stealing in his junior year, that his Catholic family saw it as the ultimate disgrace, and that they moved neighbourhoods. When Tim asks what it did to him, Rick briefly tells how, with a wise uncle's help, he put the past behind him. He does not overdramatise; his story shows that developmental crises are normal and that how people interpret and manage them is what matters.
sections.simple: Helpers always disclose themselves indirectly through their manner, but direct self-disclosure is a deliberate challenge skill. Research on it is mixed, partly because studies define it differently. It works well as modelling, as in addiction programmes, and carries the message 'You can do it too', but it is a form of intimacy that some clients find hard.
keyPoints: Indirect disclosure is constant (Strong & Claiborne); manage impressions.
Research on direct disclosure is mixed; Henretty & Levitt: multiple definitions hamper analysis.

sections.heading: Guidelines for Helper Self-Disclosure
sections.detailed:
Current research gives no definitive answers, but offers commonsense guidelines. Because clients sometimes misinterpret helpers' disclosures and their intent, caution is needed. Egan's guidelines are:

1. Make sure disclosures are appropriate. Sharing is appropriate if it helps clients reach treatment goals; do not disclose more than necessary; exhibitionistic disclosure is plainly inappropriate. Jeffrey (2004) gives outrageous examples, such as a helper discussing her own father-daughter issues, guilt over disappointing a parent, religious issues and love life; the client switched to a therapist who said nothing about herself. Disclosure should be a natural part of helping, not a gambit. Rick's disclosure gives Tim a developmental lens on the "bad things" that happened, while making clear Rick is not excusing Tim's behaviour.

2. Make sure disclosures are culturally appropriate (Barnett; Burkard et al.; Kim et al.). Helper behaviours do not automatically transfer across cultures. Carlos hesitates to share his dual-culture experiences with Mara: her Iranian culture differs greatly from his Latin background, many of her experiences have been negative while most of his were positive, and he had integrated his Hispanic and mainstream American heritage well.

3. Be careful of timing. Premature or poorly timed disclosure can distract clients or turn them off. Rick waited a few sessions and disclosed when he saw a natural opening; experience teaches what natural openings look like.

4. Keep disclosure selective and focused. Do not distract clients with rambling stories. A counsellor working with a depressed, overworked first-year clinical-psychology graduate student launches into reminiscences about his own grad-school busyness and despair; selected bits might help, but rambling meets the helper's needs rather than the client's. Rick's disclosure was selective and focused.

5. Don't disclose too frequently. Too-frequent disclosure can make clients see helpers as self-centred, phony or immature, or suspect hidden motives. Had Rick shared every parallel, Tim might have wondered who was helper and who was client.

6. Do not burden the client. A novice shared his own sexual experiences to put a client with sexual problems at ease; the client replied that he had enough trouble with his own problems. The novice disclosed too much too soon, caught up in his willingness to disclose rather than its usefulness. In extreme cases intimate disclosure can appear seductive.

7. Remain flexible. Take each client separately and adapt disclosures to clients and situations. When asked, clients say they want helpers to disclose, but not every client in every situation wants or benefits from it. Rick's natural disclosure was still a thoughtful decision.

Reviewers of Farber's (2006) book (Hamilton, Del Castillo & Stiles, 2007) concluded that readers absorb much information but find few definitive answers, appropriately so; Henretty and Levitt's (2010) extensive review agrees. Egan says these broad principles and cautions will have to do for now and, given human complexity, perhaps forever.

sections.heading: Making Suggestions and Giving Recommendations
sections.detailed:
Egan now turns to more direct approaches. Because client self-responsibility is a key value, some version of Thaler and Sunstein's (2008) "libertarian paternalism" applies to almost every form of challenge: even direct challenges leave decision making in the client's hands.

The section opens with libertarian imperatives flowing from respect and empowerment: don't tell clients what to do, don't take over their lives, let them make their own decisions. But suggestions and recommendations are not forbidden. Some clients, more in some cultures than others, expect or want explicit guidance, and guidance can be given without robbing clients of self-responsibility. There is a natural tension between wanting clients to manage their lives better and respecting their freedom. Where helpers have built strong, respectful relationships, stronger, more direct interventions make sense, and suggestions can stimulate problem-managing action; helpers move from counselling mode to a guidance role. Research shows clients generally follow recommendations that are clearly related to the problem, challenge their strengths, and are not too difficult. Effective helpers can give suggestions, recommendations and even directives without robbing clients of autonomy or integrity.

Cummings's work (1979, 2000) with substance abusers is a classic example. He listened intently during the first half of the first session; then, using training, acumen and "the third, fourth, fifth and sixth ears", he would discern some unresolved wish or long-gone dream deep in the client and ignite a desire to look at it again, knowing that if he did not touch the right nerve he would lose the client. He found the desire for a better life present, however faint, in most clients. He used basic and advanced empathy to show he understood their plight, longings and games; they knew every game, but so did he. Near the end of the first session he told them they could have a second session, which they invariably wanted, only when they were "clean", timed to the withdrawal period of their substance. They protested and played games, but he stayed firm. The directive "Get clean, then return" was part of therapy, and most returned clean. Egan adds that no approach is right for everyone.

Suggestions, advice and directives need not be taken literally; they can stimulate clients to create their own package. A mother told to let her teenage son have his say instead of interrupting and arguing made a contract: each would listen and summarise the other. It produced "useful monologues" and ended shouting matches, and she hoped to turn it into dialogue. In everyday life people freely give advice, but helpers must be cautious: suggestions, advice and directives are not for novices, and knowing when they will work takes much experience and savvy.

Clients tend to follow recommendations that fit the problem, use their strengths and are not too hard. Cummings's 'get clean, then return' shows a firm directive that worked, but such moves are not for novices.
