sections.heading: Stronger Medicine: Confrontation
sections.detailed:
Some clients keep dragging their feet and stay stuck. Those who do not want to change, or to pay its price, may simply end the relationship; those who stay range from mildly to extremely reluctant and resistant (dealt with in Chapter 7), or are collaborative on some issues and reluctant on others. Hester will work on career development but refuses to work on interpersonal and work relationships, although relationship building is part of the career package. She calls relationships her private world, dealt with inside her head and nobody else's business. Her coach tentatively checks whether she means relationships do not affect her career, asks about the forum in which she handles them, and finally notes that this may put their conversation at a standstill; they go on to discuss how putting critical issues off limits affects a therapeutic dialogue.

If inviting self-challenge is one end of the continuum, what is at the other, and where does respecting clients' right to be themselves stop and placing demands on them begin? Because this is a values issue, helpers differ theoretically and personally in their willingness to confront. Lowenstein (1993) used what he called "traumatic confrontation" (Egan questions the name) to make youths face their dysfunctional behaviour; a 12-year-old who turned to crime after his father disappeared at first denied everything but then faced the situation.

Patterson, Grenny, McMillian and Switzer (2004) say "crucial confrontations" are needed when people fail to meet clear, realistic expectations set with or for them; to confront means to hold someone accountable face to face. People who break promises, violate expectations or behave badly should expect confrontation. In counselling, confrontation focuses on the person's failure to meet his or her own expectations or the legitimate expectations of the culture or community in which he or she lives.

Helpers confront to "make the case" for more effective living. Confrontation is not a "do this or else" ultimatum; more often it ensures clients understand what not changing means: the consequences of persisting in dysfunctional patterns or the cost of missing opportunities. Like strong medicine, it is another way of caring for the client, but must be used sparingly and carefully. Confrontation should be empathic and respectful, should empower the client and lead to action, and must not be used by helpers to vent frustration on reluctant and resistant clients.

Like strong medicine, it is a form of caring but must be used sparingly, respectfully and never to vent the helper's frustration.

sections.heading: Encouragement
sections.detailed:
Egan ends on a positive note. If the purpose of challenge is to help clients move forward and encouragement ("sugar") works as well as challenge ("vinegar"), why do we hear so little about it? The analogy is imperfect, since many clients find invitations to self-challenge refreshing and stimulating, and challenge does not preclude encouragement. Encouragement is itself a mild form of challenge, a nudge. It is also a form of support, and research shows that support is one of the main ingredients of successful therapy.

Rollnick and Miller (1995) introduced motivational interviewing (MI), now supported by a large literature of theory, research and case studies. Originally for addictive behaviour, it has been adapted to a much wider range of problems, and much of its literature highlights the main elements of a problem-management approach. Miller and Rollnick (2004) define it as a directive, person-centred clinical method for helping clients resolve ambivalence and move ahead with change, usable as preparation for treatment, a freestanding brief intervention, an enduring clinical style, or a fallback when motivational obstacles arise. It can therefore be used at any stage or task of the problem-management framework, and emphasises respect, empathy, self-empowerment and self-healing.

Because "informing" clients, for example about consequences of their behaviour, is part of MI, it is admittedly directive but with a light touch. Norcross (2010) calls it a person-centred directive therapy that expresses empathy and rolls with resistance to help clients explore and resolve ambivalence. The spirit of encouragement, rather than confrontation, pervades it. Typically clients (for instance, pregnant women who smoke or drink) receive personal feedback on their problem (how smoking affects their lungs and the harm smoking and drinking can do to the fetus); personal responsibility is discussed and advice on managing the problem offered. Clients are encouraged to find motives, incentives or levers of change that make sense to them and to choose change options that fit. Intrinsic motives ("I want to be free") are emphasised over extrinsic ones ("I'll get in trouble if I don't change"). Clients get help identifying obstacles and ways to overcome them. Empathy is used extensively, both as a value and as empathic responding. Self-determination is at the heart of MI (Vansteenkiste & Sheldon, 2006).

Common sense says realistic encouragement belongs in any helping skill set and, like most skills, can be used at any stage: to identify and talk about problems and unused opportunities, review possibilities, set goals, act, and overcome obstacles. Effective encouragement is not patronising, is not the same as sympathy, does not rob clients of autonomy, and respects their self-healing abilities. It is "a fully human nudge in the right direction".
sections.simple: Encouragement is a mild challenge, a nudge, and a form of support, which research links to successful therapy. Motivational interviewing is a directive but person-centred method that uses empathy, feedback and intrinsic motives to help clients resolve ambivalence about change. Good encouragement is realistic, not patronising, not sympathy, and respects autonomy.

practice.answer: Advanced empathy is sensing and sharing the fuller message, or the message behind the message, that the client is only half saying or is scarcely aware of (building on Rogers). Because clients may not recognise themselves at once, it creates mild disequilibrium and so acts as a challenge, e.g. hearing hurt beneath Gordon's anger.

Blind spots are things people fail to see or choose to ignore that keep them from identifying and managing problems or developing opportunities. They are part of the human condition; we easily see others' blind spots but not our own (Van Hecke), and they obstruct effective decision making.

Heffernan's term for choosing to stay in the dark: 'I could find out, but I don't want to.' Choosing not to know makes us powerless, but because the blindness is willed it can be changed. Ilia, who avoids learning her probation conditions, is Egan's example.

practice.q: What is libertarian paternalism in the context of challenge?
practice.answer: An idea from Thaler and Sunstein that Egan applies to nearly every form of challenge: helpers may make direct challenges, suggestions or recommendations, but decision making remains in the client's hands, protecting self-responsibility.

Sternberg described four self-beliefs that make smart people do stupid things: egocentrism (it is all about me), omniscience (I know everything), omnipotence (I can do whatever I want) and invulnerability (I will not be caught or can escape any fix).

practice.q: Explain the targets of self-challenge identified by Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction: Egan says counsellors should help clients challenge whatever stands in the way of managing problems or developing opportunities. Some self-challenge is self-critical, some self-enhancing (Chang).

Targets: (1) Self-defeating mind-sets, relatively permanent beliefs, assumptions and prejudices, e.g. Candace's stereotype or Ellis's irrational beliefs such as 'I must be problemless'. (2) Self-limiting internal behaviour, chosen thinking acts like dysfunctional daydreaming (John) or automatic fault-finding (Nadia). (3) Self-defeating expression of emotion: bottling up (Sheila), running riot, or flying off the handle (Arthur). (4) Dysfunctional external behaviour, including not acting, e.g. Clarence refusing promotion, Ryan's aggression. (5) Distorted understanding of the world, e.g. Sandra misreading her husband. (6) Discrepancies, such as say-versus-do (Clarissa). (7) Unused strengths and resources, internal and external; even irrationalities hold strengths (Driscoll). (8) The predictable dishonesties of everyday life: distortions, games and excuses. A final category is participating fully in helping.

Why it matters: mind-sets tend to drive or leak into external behaviour, so Egan's principle is to invite clients to turn outmoded, self-limiting mind-sets into liberating perspectives that drive action. Internal behaviours are chosen, so they can be re-chosen; Bella's 'wearing black inside' shows how one new perspective can shift a life. Discrepancies and dishonesties are usually challenged gently, as in the Clarissa dialogue.

Conclusion: In practice these targets mix, as Minerva shows, and often lie behind blind spots the client does not notice.

practice.q: Describe the kinds of blind spots discussed by Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction: Blind spots are what we fail to see or choose to ignore, blocking problem management and opportunity development. Egan describes several 'flavours'.

Lack of awareness: some things clients simply do not know, e.g. Serge's unrecognised talents or Casper's acerbic style. Unawareness comes in degrees.

Failure to think things through: haphazard reasoning, driven by emotion (Kim and Lea), habit or laziness, and failure to foresee consequences (Clancy).

Self-deception: not wanting to know because knowing would demand change (Goleman; Giannetti); Stan's flirting cost his engagement.

Choosing to stay in the dark: Heffernan's willful blindness; Ilia avoids her probation conditions; evasiveness may signal self-concealment.

Knowing, not caring and failing to see consequences: Tanel keeps nagging despite growing resentment.

Implication for helpers: some blind spots seem unintentional and others self-inflicted, but both block change. Van Hecke notes that people readily see others' blind spots while missing their own, so clients may be perceptive about others yet need help seeing themselves. Helping clients deal with blind spots can prevent damage, limit damage already done and turn problems into opportunities.

Conclusion: 'Blind spot' is elastic but has face validity. Lester shows the full dysfunctional package, Bernice turns prejudice into opportunity, and Box 6.1 offers questions to surface blind spots.

practice.q: Discuss information sharing as a challenging skill, with its cautions.
practice.answer:
Introduction: Clients sometimes cannot explore problems, set goals or act because they lack information. Information sharing, including correcting misinformation, is a challenging skill because it creates new perspectives or shows how to act.

Uses: It helps at every stage: early (knowing others have faced the problem), in goal setting, and in implementation (knowing common obstacles). It can be supportive, as when SIDS information eases a parent's self-blame, or both relieving and painful, as with Adrian learning about the educational pyramid and then facing the world of work. It is especially useful when lack of accurate information causes or worsens the problem; doctors and counsellors may team up, as with Doug's prostate-cancer decision.

Cautions: be tactful with shocking news and help with disequilibrium; do not overwhelm; keep it clear and relevant; check for misunderstanding; be supportive and help process it; never confuse information giving with advice giving.

Example in detail: Adrian, a hardworking student rejected by every graduate programme, believed most students went on to graduate school because his friends did. Statistics on the shrinking percentage of students at each level showed that finishing college already placed him in an elite group, but also left him suddenly facing the world of work. In Doug's case neither doctor nor counsellor chose his treatment; they helped him carry the burden of choosing.

Conclusion: Information widens clients' perspective while leaving the choice to them.

practice.q: What guidelines does Egan give for helper self-disclosure?
practice.answer:
Introduction: Research on direct helper self-disclosure is mixed, partly because of differing definitions (Henretty & Levitt), so Egan offers commonsense guidelines.

1. Appropriate: disclose only to serve treatment goals and no more than necessary; avoid exhibitionism (Jeffrey's examples).
2. Culturally appropriate: behaviours do not transfer automatically across cultures (Carlos and Mara).
3. Timing: premature disclosure distracts; wait for a natural opening, as Rick did.
4. Selective and focused: avoid rambling reminiscence that meets the helper's needs.
5. Not too frequent: clients may see the helper as self-centred, phony or immature.
6. Do not burden the client: a novice's sexual disclosures overwhelmed a client; intimate disclosure can seem seductive.
7. Remain flexible: adapt to each client and situation.

Why caution is needed: clients sometimes misinterpret helpers' disclosures and their intent. Done well, as with Beth in a drug programme or Rick with Tim, disclosure models openness, gives clients courage to talk, and offers a new lens on their problems; Rick's developmental perspective helped Tim see that how crises are interpreted and managed is what matters.

Conclusion: Disclosure is challenging because it is intimate and implies 'You can do it, too'; reviews (Farber; Hamilton et al.) give few definitive answers, so these principles must suffice.

Introduction: Some clients drag their feet; they range from mildly to extremely reluctant, or are reluctant only on some issues, like Hester, who keeps relationships off limits.

Nature: Where respect for clients ends and placing demands begins is a values question, so helpers differ in willingness to confront. Lowenstein used 'traumatic confrontation' with youths. Patterson et al. describe 'crucial confrontations', holding someone accountable face to face when clear, realistic expectations are not met. In counselling, confrontation focuses on failure to meet one's own expectations or the legitimate expectations of one's community.

Purpose: Helpers confront to 'make the case' for more effective living, not to issue ultimatums, making sure clients understand the consequences of not changing.

Guidelines: Like strong medicine it is a form of caring but must be used sparingly and carefully; it should be empathic, respectful, empowering and action-oriented, never a way to vent frustration.

The Hester dialogue shows the style: the coach checks tentatively whether she means relationships do not affect her career, asks where she deals with them, and finally notes that keeping them off limits may bring the conversation to a standstill. This leads to a discussion of how putting critical issues off limits affects a therapeutic dialogue, a confrontation that stays respectful and collaborative.

Conclusion: Confrontation is the far end of the challenge continuum, used only when gentler invitations fail.

practice.q: Discuss the concept of self-challenge and the goals and targets of challenging as described by Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction
Egan begins from the idea that helping is about change and change involves choices. Chapters 6 and 7 apply the 'choice architecture' of Chapter 5, and inviting clients to challenge themselves is a stronger form of nudging. Helping clients place demands on themselves is among the most important things a helper does.

The basic concept
Although little therapy research addresses self-challenge, Egan argues that centuries of human-development wisdom offer practice-based evidence that should balance evidence-based practice. Failure to challenge can be devastating, as in operating rooms where 60% of one survey's respondents found it hard to speak up. Reasonable self-challenge is part of maturity and follows from the values of self-responsibility and a bias for action. Belinda, who recognised her overprotective parenting in an article, shows ideal self-initiated challenge.

Since helping is a constructive social-influence process, challenge is central, yet the stance stays pro-client and collaborative. All effective helping mixes support and challenge: challenge alone is harsh, support alone can be empty. Martin and Trevino argue that helping adds value when it is somewhat discordant with clients' self-theories; Claiborn's review found discrepant views improve outcomes by changing how clients construe problems. Egan prefers 'challenge' to 'confrontation' because it is more acceptable, and Finn stresses compassion and firmness. Helpers help clients see how their beliefs-values-norms drivers shape decisions rather than attacking those drivers.

Goals
The overall goal is reality testing invested in a better future. One goal is to change ways of thinking, expressing emotion and acting that keep clients stuck (Wei & Ku). A parallel, upbeat goal is to help clients find possibilities, discover unused resources, invest them, spell out a better future and commit to action, making the counsellor a 'catalyst for a better future'.

Targets
Self-challenge can be self-critical or self-enhancing (Chang). The targets are: self-defeating mind-sets, such as prejudice (Candace), Ellis's irrational beliefs like being problemless (Allison) and Sternberg's four fallacies; self-limiting internal behaviour, such as John's daydreaming or Nadia's fault-finding; self-defeating emotional expression, from bottling up (Sheila) to flying off the handle (Arthur), linked to emotion regulation (Berking et al.); dysfunctional external behaviour, including failing to act (Clarence) and aggression (Ryan); distorted understanding of the world (Sandra); discrepancies such as say-versus-do (Clarissa); unused strengths and resources, where even irrationalities can be strengths (Driscoll); and the predictable dishonesties of everyday life, namely distortions (Nancy), games (Kennard's 'Yes, but') and excuses (Roberto). Helping clients participate fully in helping is a further target.

Integration
Minerva shows these targets mixed together: a distrustful mind-set, suspicious internal behaviour, coldness, defensiveness, a trust discrepancy, a fault-finding game, misreading friends and guarded participation, all without awareness. Hayes's ACT adds a caution: rather than warring with bad thoughts, clients can defuse them and commit to purposeful living.

Conclusion
For Egan, self-challenge is collaborative, caring and future-oriented. It targets whatever blocks problem management and opportunity development, and it always pairs challenge with support so clients can move from new perspectives to new behaviour.

practice.q: Explain advanced empathy and its different forms, with examples.
practice.answer:
Introduction
Advanced empathy is the first of Egan's indirect approaches to client self-challenge. Drawing on Rogers's idea that empathy may sense meanings the client is scarcely aware of, Egan defines it as capturing and sharing the fuller message or the message behind the message.

Nature and difference from basic empathy
Accurate basic empathy is recognised immediately ('Yes, that's what I meant'). Advanced empathy reaches more covert messages, so clients may not recognise themselves at once and experience some disequilibrium; this makes it a challenge, inviting a closer look at oneself. When the helper notes hurt mixed with Gordon's anger at his ex-wife, Gordon admits she can still get to him, deepening the discussion. Helpers ask themselves what the client is only half saying, hinting at, saying confusedly, or conveying covertly. Advanced empathy stays with what the client actually expresses; it is not interpretation or 'psyching out'. It also uncovers buried strengths and opportunities. In the soldier example, Chaplain A's basic empathy leaves the soldier resigned, while Chaplain B picks up 'not as flashy', helping him see he may be overlooked and discuss marketing himself in line with his values.

Form 1: Making the implied explicit
The most basic form. A divorced client talks without enthusiasm about calling his ex-wife. Counselor A's basic response stalls him; Counselor B notes the lack of enthusiasm, and he admits guilt and a caretaking pattern, then brightens about a business idea. No highlight is good in itself; it is judged by whether it helps the client see the need to act.

Form 2: Identifying themes
Themes may involve feelings, thoughts, behaviours or experiences. A supervisor helps a trainee see that his sessions are all basic empathy and that his underlying theme is 'playing it safe' from fear of being pushy.

Form 3: Making missing connections
Clients tell stories in a hit-or-miss way. Chu Hua's weak strategies are linked to half-hearted goals; Owen moves from excuses to owning his porn addiction; Joanna's ingratiating style is linked to low influence; Dieter's anxiety to perfectionism out of place in Kenya; and John discovers that family squabbling multiplies his stress.

Form 4: Sharing educated hunches
Hunches grow more educated with maturity and experience. They help clients see the bigger picture (perfectionism 'spreading'), go deeper ('betrayed' rather than 'let down'), see implications (a project that should be shut down), open up hinted areas (sexual matters), see what is overlooked (no health power of attorney) and own their stories ('already decided to quit').

Guidelines
Hunches must rest on identifiable experiential and behavioural clues; empathy is no licence to infer at will or impose favourite theories. Constructive advanced empathy requires emotional intelligence and social competence.

Conclusion
Advanced empathy is a gentle but powerful challenge: grounded in the client's own message, it helps clients see what they half know and turn blind spots into new perspectives and action.

practice.q: Critically discuss helper self-disclosure and the direct approaches to challenge (suggestions, confrontation and encouragement).
practice.answer:
Introduction
After advanced empathy and information sharing, Egan discusses helper self-disclosure as the last indirect approach, then more direct approaches, all under 'libertarian paternalism' (Thaler & Sunstein): even direct challenges leave decisions with the client.

Helper self-disclosure
Helpers always disclose indirectly through looks, movements and words (Strong & Claiborne), so they must manage impressions. Direct disclosure is more contested: Henretty and Levitt note that multiple definitions make research hard to compare; some studies find it frightens or burdens clients, others that clients see disclosers as down-to-earth and honest. It works well as modelling in AA and drug programmes (Beth). It is challenging because it is intimate and implies 'You can do it, too'. Rick's brief, undramatic story to Tim shows developmental crises are normal. Guidelines: keep it appropriate and goal-related, culturally appropriate, well timed, selective and focused, infrequent, non-burdening and flexible. Reviews (Farber; Hamilton et al.) offer few definitive answers.

Suggestions and recommendations
Libertarian imperatives say: don't tell clients what to do or take over their lives. Yet guidance is not forbidden, and some cultures expect it. Within strong, respectful relationships, helpers can move into a guidance role. Clients follow recommendations that relate to the problem, challenge their strengths and are not too difficult. Cummings ignited substance abusers' buried dreams and then told them 'Get clean, then return'; most came back clean. Suggestions can also stimulate clients' own solutions, like the mother's listening contract with her son. Such interventions are not for novices.

Confrontation
For foot-dragging clients like Hester, confrontation is 'stronger medicine'. How far to push is a values issue; Lowenstein used 'traumatic confrontation', and Patterson et al. define confronting as holding someone accountable face to face. In counselling it targets failures to meet one's own or the community's legitimate expectations and 'makes the case' for change by clarifying the costs of not changing. It must be sparing, empathic, respectful, empowering and action-oriented, never a vent for frustration.

Encouragement
Encouragement is a mild challenge and a form of support, a main ingredient of successful therapy. Motivational interviewing (Rollnick & Miller) is a directive, person-centred method for resolving ambivalence, using feedback, intrinsic motives, help with obstacles and extensive empathy, with self-determination at its heart. Effective encouragement is realistic, not patronising, not sympathy, and preserves autonomy.

Critical evaluation
Egan's approach is pragmatic: research is inconclusive on disclosure and no directive fits everyone. His safeguard is consistent: every approach is judged by whether it serves the client's goals and preserves self-responsibility.

Egan's caution also applies throughout: no approach is right for everyone, and directives in particular need experience and savvy to know when they will work.

Conclusion
From self-disclosure to confrontation and encouragement, Egan offers a graded set of tools, all aimed at moving clients from new perspectives to new behaviour while keeping them in charge.

practice.q: Explain the predictable dishonesties of everyday life and how helpers can address them.
practice.answer:
Introduction: Egan uses this phrase for the distortions, evasions, games, tricks, excuse making and smoke screens that keep clients and everyone stuck.

Two-edged nature: Little dishonesties help us cope, but carry a price, especially as a preferred strategy; blaming others saves face but blocks self-responsibility. The aim is not to strip defences, which could be dangerous, but to help clients cope more creatively.

Distortions: self-serving views of reality, e.g. Arnie seeing a caring supervisor as aloof, Edna seeing her counsellor as divine, Nancy equating getting her way with being liked.

Games and smoke screens: clients rewarded for games continue them (Berne). Kennard plays 'Yes, but'; Dora acts helpless then resents help. Helpers should create an atmosphere that discourages games.

Excuses: universal (Snyder, Higgins & Stucky) and sometimes useful, but used to avoid problems, as when Roberto sabotages Maria's career 'for her own good'.

Process example: with Nancy, the counsellor first removes the implied distortion that only she cares about their son, then probes how home decisions came to rest with her, and develops a hunch that the conflict with Milan is as much about power and getting her own way as about parenting. Fearful clients use communication in order not to communicate, so helpers watch for smoke screens from early sessions.

Conclusion: Skilled helpers are caring and empathic but do not let themselves be conned.

Motivational interviewing, introduced by Rollnick and Miller, is a directive, person-centred method for helping clients resolve ambivalence and move ahead with change. It uses personal feedback, empathy and intrinsic motives, rolls with resistance (Norcross), and places self-determination at its heart.
